findings.claim: from the Latin compositum, something put together
findings.because: Compote comes through Old French composte from Latin composita, the feminine of compositus (a mixture), not the neuter compositum.
findings.fix: French, from the Latin composita, something put together

findings.claim: Grapes thinned from the vine in early summer
findings.because: Verjus grapes come from the green harvest just before or at veraison, which in the northern hemisphere is July into August: midsummer, not early summer.
findings.fix: Grapes thinned from the vine in midsummer

findings.claim: Emilia-Romagna, Italy
findings.because: Saba (sapa) is just as traditional in the Marche and Sardinia. Naming only Emilia-Romagna reads as an exclusive origin a guest from Sardinia could correct.
findings.fix: Emilia-Romagna, Marche and Sardinia, from the Latin sapa, cooked must

findings.claim: made from sherry and aged for years in oak barrels
findings.because: Only the Reserva (2 years) and Gran Reserva (10 years) grades are aged for years. The basic Vinagre de Jerez grade needs just 6 months, and the card's own why says so. A server will say 'for years' about the house bottle too.
findings.fix: made from sherry and aged in oak barrels, often for years

findings.claim: with the pieces still whole
findings.because: Many compotes, including the rhubarb on this card's own menu line and most berry compotes, partly collapse. 'Still whole' promises the guest intact fruit. What makes it compote is that it is loose and chunky rather than set or strained.
findings.fix: with the fruit still in soft pieces

findings.claim: Fruit gently stewed in syrup so the pieces keep their shape
findings.because: A test-taker could also accept this for its section neighbor Mostarda, which is whole fruit candied in syrup. The gist leaves out the thing that marks compote: it is loose, spoonable and not set.
findings.fix: Fruit gently stewed in light syrup, loose and spoonable, never set

findings.claim: Seared foie gras, verjus grapes, brioche
findings.because: Real menus do not say 'verjus grapes'. It reads as a grape variety, and a guest may ask which grape that is. Menus list verjus as a sauce or glaze, or next to the fruit.
findings.fix: Seared foie gras, grapes, verjus, brioche

findings.claim: It tastes of raisins and honey
findings.because: Saba is grape must alone. When a server says 'honey' at the table, a guest can take it as an ingredient, and someone who avoids honey will turn the dish down, or ask, for no reason.
findings.fix: It tastes of rich, jammy raisins

findings.claim: brighter than any berry jam
findings.because: This is an oversell and a matter of taste, and a guest can argue with it. The line before it already says what the preserve tastes like.
findings.fix: with a pleasant bitter edge

findings.claim: "scallion"
findings.because: Many kimchi recipes thicken the chili paste with a cooked flour porridge. It is often sweet rice flour, but wheat flour is common too, especially in home-style and commercial kimchi. Wheat is something a guest with an allergy needs flagged, and the list does not mention it. Scallion does not matter to an allergic guest, so swapping it out keeps the list at 7 items.
findings.fix: sometimes wheat or rice flour

findings.claim: KOR-nee-shohn
findings.because: American dictionaries (Merriam-Webster) give the final syllable as -shahn, and that is how US dining rooms say it; -shohn sounds like the French nasal and will make a new hire hesitate.
findings.fix: KOR-nee-shahn

findings.claim: "sometimes coconut", "sometimes mustard seed"
findings.because: The why says fresh Indian chutneys are part of the family, and South Indian peanut chutney is a common one, so a peanut flag is missing for a guest with that allergy. Swap out mustard seed, which is the less critical flag.
findings.fix: "sometimes coconut", "sometimes peanut"

findings.claim: "rice"
findings.because: Not every miso has rice in it: hatcho and other mame miso grow the koji on soybeans alone, and mugi miso uses barley in place of rice. Listing rice with no qualifier says it is always there.
findings.fix: "often rice"

findings.claim: KOR-nee-shohn
findings.because: American dining rooms, and Merriam-Webster, end the word on an 'ahn' sound (KOR-nih-shahn), not 'ohn'. A new hire who says 'shohn' will sound off to guests and to the kitchen.
findings.fix: KOR-nee-shahn

findings.claim: it adds a rich, almost buttery depth
findings.because: Miso does not taste buttery. It tastes salty and savory. Glazes like the black cod one often do have real butter in them, so a guest who avoids dairy could hear 'buttery' as a statement about the dish, and the server has no way to answer that.
findings.fix: it adds a rich, savory depth

findings.claim: In the dish it reads as savory depth, not as fishiness.
findings.because: 'Reads as' is writer's jargon. A nervous new hire saying it aloud sounds like they are reading off a card, and guests will not understand it right away. Plain words do the same job.
findings.fix: In the dish it just tastes deep and savory, not fishy.

findings.claim: "often onion"
findings.because: Peanut chutney is a standard South Indian table chutney, and roasted peanut or cashew often thickens herb and coconut chutneys. A server asked about nuts needs peanut flagged. Onion matters to no guest with an allergy, and the list is already at its 7-item cap, so swap it out.
findings.fix: sometimes peanut

findings.claim: "it adds a rich, almost buttery depth"
findings.because: Miso is soybean, salt and grain, with no dairy in it. A guest who avoids milk can hear "buttery" as a sign that butter is in the dish, and miso glazes are often finished with real butter, which makes the word even more misleading.
findings.fix: it adds a rich, rounded depth

findings.claim: warm spices like caraway and cumin
findings.because: The defining spices of Tunisian harissa, as in the UNESCO 2022 inscription and the card's own lexicon entry, are caraway and coriander. Many recipes add cumin, but it is not what defines the paste.
findings.fix: warm spices like caraway and coriander

findings.claim: "cumin"
findings.because: Cumin is a common addition but not part of the classic formula (dried chili, garlic, caraway, coriander, salt, olive oil). Listing it flat implies every harissa has it.
findings.fix: often cumin

findings.claim: which is usually unsmoked and milder
findings.because: Sweet pimentón (dulce), the most common kind, has no more heat than ordinary sweet paprika. What sets it apart is smoke and depth, not heat, so "milder" tells a server the Spanish kind is hotter.
findings.fix: which is usually unsmoked and flatter in flavor

findings.claim: Large crystals added at the last second stay whole
findings.because: Fleur de sel, which the same sentence names, is fine and damp, not large crystals or flakes. It crunches because it is added dry and last, not because the crystals are big.
findings.fix: Crystals added at the last second stay whole

findings.claim: Dry-aged strip, bone marrow butter, flaky salt
findings.because: The menu line must carry the term or an alias as written, and "flaky salt" is neither: the card lists no aliases. "Flaky salt" is how real menus actually print it, and it is the most common finishing salt, so keep the line and add the alias rather than forcing the stiffer "finishing salt" onto a menu.
findings.fix: aliases: ["Flaky Salt"] (line unchanged)

findings.claim: Chutney is not linked to Chow-Chow (Southern section), the other jarred sweet-sour relish on the roster. Guests and new hires really do mix the two up: 'is chow-chow a kind of chutney?' The link to Mostarda also runs one way only: Mostarda lists Chutney as a confusion, but Chutney has Mostarda only in seeAlsoTerms.

Across the section the gists average about 64.6 characters and the traps about 62, so 'pick the longest' still wins more than chance.

findings.claim: Accuracy. The gist ('salted and aged a year or more') and the why ('in barrels for a year or longer') state a year as the defining minimum. Premium first-press brands age about 12 to 18 months, but much commercial fish sauce ferments for well under a year (6 to 12 months is common). A server would be repeating something that is not true of many bottles.

findings.claim: The alias 'Flaky Salt' names one kind of finishing salt, not the same thing sold under another name. The card's own why names fleur de sel, which is moist crystals, not flakes, and the guest line 'It's a flaky salt' carries the same narrowing. The aliases rule is 'other names the SAME thing is sold under'.

critic.notes: Every roster row has a card, and ids and terms match. The prose averages 665 characters a card, under the 720 ceiling. The heaviest cards are Pimentón at 771 and Mostarda at 740, both inside the 900 per-card cap. The Banyuls known packet error is covered: its trap reads 'eastern France' and matches /east/i. No verdict words, no em or en dashes and no banned food-safety substrings turned up. No gist or trap uses a word from its card's mayNotAppearInGistOrTraps list. Every card with an accented letter or a hard name has a say. Every card with confusedWithTerms has a notThis. No two gists or guest lines are hard to tell apart; the closest pairs, Balsamic/Saba and Jam/Compote/Marmalade, each say what sets them apart. Operator notes: (1) Compote lists Coulis as a confusion. Check that the Coulis card in the sauces section links back to Compote. (2) Both Balsamic and Saba could reasonably add Gastrique or Agrodolce to seeAlsoTerms, since guests call balsamic reduction a gastrique, but that is optional. (3) The Mostarda origin says the word comes from 'mosto, grape must'. The usual etymology is Latin mustum ardens, 'burning must', which is better and still checkable.

findings.claim: Pimentón is Spanish and smoked
findings.because: Pimentón is simply Spanish paprika; only pimentón de la Vera is oak-smoked, while pimentón de Murcia is unsmoked. The roster's own Pimentón card (fd_0283) says 'often smoked' and names Murcia in its origin, so this card contradicts the card it points to.
findings.fix: Not smoked paprika. Spanish pimentón is often smoked; this is French, unsmoked, fruitier.

findings.claim: The bite is gone; it tastes more like balsamic.
findings.because: The guest line may not carry a semicolon (house rule: no brackets, colons or semicolons in guest); a server reads this aloud as two sentences anyway.
findings.fix: The bite is gone. It tastes more like balsamic.

findings.claim: Pimentón is Spanish and smoked
findings.because: Only pimentón de la Vera is smoked; pimentón de Murcia is sun-dried and unsmoked. Stated flat, a server will tell a guest every pimentón is smoked, which the deck's own Pimentón card (three spices under one word) will contradict.
findings.fix: Not smoked paprika. Spain's pimentón is usually smoked; this is French and fruitier.

findings.claim: Cloves aged warm and damp for weeks until soft, jet black and sweet
findings.because: At 67 characters the gist ties the longest trap (67) and runs 6 over the other (61); the brief says the gist must never be the longest option and to shorten the gist rather than pad a trap. 'Jet' adds nothing a test-taker needs.
findings.fix: Cloves aged warm and damp for weeks until soft, black and sweet

dispositions.reason: notThis now reads 'Spanish pimentón is often smoked' instead of 'is Spanish and smoked', since only pimentón de la Vera is oak-smoked while pimentón de Murcia is unsmoked, matching the roster's Pimentón card.
Guest line split at the semicolon into two sentences: 'The bite is gone. It tastes more like balsamic.'
Same change as pantry-1-fact-1: notThis softened to 'often smoked' so a server no longer tells guests every pimentón is smoked.
Dropped 'jet' from the gist; it is now 63 characters against traps of 61 and 67, so the gist is no longer the longest option.

problems.issue: No `level` on the card. The roster row carries none, so rule 9 makes it the writer's call, and validate.mjs refuses a written card without one.
problems.fix: Add `level: 3`. Espelette is fine-dining vocabulary, rarer on American menus than Pimentón (2), and sits with Crudo and Mostarda at Sous Chef.

problems.issue: No `level` on the card; validate.mjs refuses a written card without one.
problems.fix: Add `level: 3`. A specialist Japanese condiment that needs a sentence and shows up beside Crudo (3); not rare enough for 4.

problems.issue: No `level` on the card; validate.mjs refuses a written card without one.
problems.fix: Add `level: 2`. Black garlic is now common at a good restaurant and guests ask about it every night; it takes one sentence, the standard for Chef de Partie, alongside Miso and Harissa.

problems.issue: Espelette lists Pimentón under confusedWithTerms but Pimentón does not link back, so the pair is linked only one way and a reader drilling Pimentón never meets the confusion. Pimentón's notThis already exists, so the reciprocal link is legal.
problems.fix: Add 'fd_0349' to Pimentón's confusedWith (keep seeAlso fd_0065, fd_0041). Optionally sharpen its notThis: 'Not Espelette, the French Basque chili that is never smoked, and not grocery paprika. Ask whether the kitchen uses sweet or hot.'

problems.issue: Menu line 'Grilled octopus, espelette, lemon aioli' opens exactly as Pimentón's line does ('Grilled octopus, olive oil potatoes, smoked pimentón'). The two cards are the section's one confusable pair, and a reader flipping both sees the same dish under both terms.
problems.fix: Give Espelette a line the Spanish card cannot own, e.g. 'Roast cod, brown butter, espelette' or 'Piperade, Bayonne ham, espelette, fried egg'.

problems.issue: seeAlsoTerms includes 'Abalone Mushroom', which has no relation to black garlic beyond mushrooms appearing in pairs; a see-also is for related cards, and this one sends the reader nowhere useful.
problems.fix: Replace 'Abalone Mushroom' with 'Caramelized' (the slow browning the why describes) or drop to two: ['Balsamic', 'Koji-Aged'].

critic.notes: Checked against the whole on-disk section (tools/derive/floor-deck/pantry.mjs, 19 written cards) plus the three new ones: all 22 roster rows have a card, no duplicate gists or guest lines, no verdict words, dashes, banned substrings, guest punctuation or guest temperatures on the three new cards, all closing-stop rules met, gist/trap length parity within 10 chars and no gist the longest option. Section mean is 672 prose chars per card (ceiling 720); new cards run 711/707/718, so no condensing needed, though Yuzu Kosho's note ('very salty as well as hot', 'pea-sized dab') restates the why and guest and is the cheapest cut if the mean ever tightens; its origin also repeats the why's 'kosho means chili'. Banyuls' knownPacketError trap matches /east/i. Facts on the new cards hold: Gorria variety and AOC 2000 for Espelette; Kyushu dialect kosho = chili; black garlic at 60 to 70 C (140 to 158 F) with no microbial step. Pimentón at 771 prose is the section's longest card, still under the 900 ceiling. Bench term worth promoting later: Ponzu (used as a Yuzu Kosho trap and a real menu word with no card). Pairs to consider linking across sections: Kimchi with Fermented (already seeAlso, arguably confusedWith Pickled); Black Garlic with Roasted as confusedWithTerms since its notThis already argues the distinction.

findings.claim: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, never fiery.
findings.because: Many vadouvan recipes, including Pondicherry ones, include dried red chili or black pepper. It is usually mild, but heat varies by producer, so 'never' is an assurance a server cannot back.
findings.fix: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, and is seldom hot.

findings.claim: "shallot", "onion", "garlic", "mustard seed", "fenugreek", "cumin", "often curry leaf"
findings.because: The aromatics are fried in oil, and traditional vadagam-style blends use sesame oil (alongside castor or coconut oil) and often urad dal lentils. Sesame is a major allergen and the list never flags it. Curry leaf is not an allergy concern, so it is the slot to give up.
findings.fix: "shallot", "onion", "garlic", "mustard seed", "fenugreek", "cumin", "oil, sometimes sesame"

findings.claim: "ume fruit", "salt", "often red shiso"
findings.because: A common commercial style, katsuo-ume, is finished with bonito flakes (fish), and honey-ume (hachimitsu umeboshi) is common too. A guest with a fish allergy needs that flagged, and the list has room for it.
findings.fix: "ume fruit", "salt", "often red shiso", "sometimes bonito flakes", "sometimes honey"

findings.claim: Too sour to eat fresh,
findings.because: Sourness is not the main reason. Raw ume are not eaten because the unripe fruit and its pit hold amygdalin, which makes them mildly toxic until they are salted or cooked. Better to leave the reason out than give a misleading one.
findings.fix: Inedible raw,

findings.claim: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, never fiery.
findings.because: Vadouvan recipes and commercial blends often include dried chili or cayenne, and its madeWith list does not rule it out. A guest who avoids heat will hear 'never fiery' as a promise, and the server cannot keep it for every kitchen's blend.
findings.fix: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, mostly mild.

findings.claim: Kitchens now make their own from beef, squid or mushrooms, and a few drops add deep, savory seasoning.
findings.because: The list leaves out fish, so a nervous server will repeat it as 'this garum is not fish'. Many modern house garums are still made from fish, and the card's own note says to ask which base this one uses. 'Add deep, savory seasoning' also sounds read off a card.
findings.fix: Chefs now ferment their own from fish, meat or mushrooms, and a few drops give deep savory flavor.

findings.claim: It makes the dish taste deeply savory and of the sea, not fishy.
findings.because: Colatura is anchovy liquid and plainly tastes of anchovy. Saying 'not fishy' oversells it, and a guest who dislikes fish may order on that promise and send the dish back.
findings.fix: It gives the dish a deep, savory taste of the sea.

findings.claim: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, never fiery.
findings.because: "Never" is an absolute assurance about heat that a guest who avoids chili could rely on. Many vadouvan blends, both house-made and bought, include red chili flakes or cayenne. The blend is usually mild, but a kitchen's version can carry some chili.
findings.fix: It tastes warm, sweet and savory, and usually mild.

findings.claim: Kitchens now make their own from beef, squid or mushrooms
findings.because: The first sentence calls it fish sauce, and the second then leaves fish out of the modern bases. A guest with a fish allergy can hear that as an assurance that this kitchen's garum is not made from fish. Many modern house garums are still fish-based, and the card's own madeWith opens with fish. This adds a few characters because it is a safety fact.
findings.fix: Kitchens now make their own from fish, squid, beef or mushrooms

findings.claim: Cooks pierce them into stews or grind them
findings.because: The card leaves out a handling fact a server should be able to state. A whole black lime simmered in a stew stays a hard, hollow shell with bitter seeds inside. It is meant to be pressed for flavor and set aside, not bitten into whole. This is the same kind of fact as the umeboshi pit note. Adding the note makes the card longer, but it is a safety fact.
findings.fix: Add note: "Cooked whole in a stew, it stays a hard shell with bitter seeds. Press it for flavor rather than biting into it."

findings.claim: The Colatura gist is hard to tell apart from the live Fish Sauce gist (fd_0281). The Fish Sauce gist reads "Amber liquid drained from anchovies salted and aged for months", and that is a TRUE description of colatura. The Colatura gist reads "Amber Italian anchovy liquid aged in barrels on the Amalfi coast". The two share amber, anchovy, liquid and aged. Whichever card is being tested, the other gist sits among the options as a defensible right answer.

I checked completeness against the brief. The roster has 27 rows: 22 written live cards in src/lib/data/floor-deck.json plus the 5 new cards here, so every row has a card. I measured the section mean at about 677 characters of prose per card with the new five included, under the 720 ceiling. By card: Colatura 663, Vadouvan 665, Umeboshi 682, Garum 722, Black Lime 766, which is the longest and could lose its note if the mean ever gets tight. A scan of all five new cards (prose and traps) for the banned words, verdict language, em and en dashes and British spelling found nothing. The one knownPacketError in the roster (fd_0267 Banyuls, east) already has its matching trap in floor-deck.traps.json.
